text: The big idea today: A tour of the workshop structure, the two-day arc, and what you will accomplish. We will name the concept, explain why it matters, practice the move, and point out the checks that tell you the work is real.

text: GitHub Learning Room - Your Complete Workshop Companion: the learner is about to begin a two-day journey into open source collaboration using GitHub, VS Code, and GitHub Copilot - all designed for screen reader and keyboard-only navigation. This guide is your starting point and table of contents for everything in this workshop.

speaker: ALEX
text: This is a two-day workshop built around one idea: you will make real contributions to a real open source project.

text: What should feel predictable before the first live session starts?

text: the live hackathon agenda is intentionally smaller than the full curriculum. Live sessions prioritize the core contribution path, while the complete chapter set remains available for self-paced preparation, catch-up, remote participation, and post-event continuation.

speaker: ALEX
text: Live core: The facilitator chooses the minimum path needed for participants to make and understand a real contribution. Async follow-up: Chapters and challenges not covered live can be completed after the session using the Learning Room, solutions, podcasts, and Slack channel. text: You learn GitHub's web interface using only your keyboard and screen reader. This is the part to say slowly: The live Day 1 core path gets you through repository navigation, issues, branches, commits, and a first pull request.

text: You move to Visual Studio Code, learn GitHub Copilot, and activate the Accessibility Agents ecosystem - 55 AI agents across 3 teams and 5 platforms that amplify every skill you built on Day 1. text: The workshop includes structured exercises across the curriculum. Every exercise is designed to be completed in 1-5 minutes, is impossible to fail, and follows the same pattern: Try It - You're done when - What success feels like.

text: if you get stuck at any point during the workshop, these resources are always available. Open a support issue at https://github.com/Community-Access/support/issues describing what you tried, what happened, and what you expected.

speaker: ALEX
text: Start with Chapter 00: Pre-Workshop Setup. The durable skill is not memorizing one screen. It is knowing how to find your footing when the screen changes.

speaker: ALEX
text: This workshop is designed so you are never left guessing what comes next. The goal is to build confidence one checkable step at a time.

speaker: ALEX
text: The useful version is not abstract; it sounds like this. A GitHub Classroom assignment link from the facilitator. Your own private Learning Room repository. Challenge issues that tell you exactly what to do. Evidence prompts that tell you what to post when you finish.

speaker: ALEX
text: Do not treat When Tools or Pages Change as decoration. GitHub.com, GitHub Classroom, VS Code, GitHub Copilot, github.dev, browser extensions, and agent tools change often. This course is actively maintained, and we use official sources and live checks wherever possible, but your screen may not always match the exact wording in a step.

speaker: ALEX
text: First, check the URL and browser tab title. Then, move by headings, landmarks, tabs, and button names instead of relying only on visual order. After that, open keyboard shortcut help (? on GitHub) or the VS Code Command Palette when a shortcut or control differs. Finally, read the surrounding labels before activating a control. Keep it that plain: know where you are, make the move, check the result.

text: How would you walk the room through that step by step?

text: Start here: Ask a facilitator or file a curriculum issue with the page link, the step that differed, and what you heard or observed.

speaker: ALEX
text: before Day 1 starts, complete Chapter 00: Pre-Workshop Setup. That chapter helps you create or verify your GitHub account, configure accessibility settings, choose a browser, install Git and VS Code, and confirm your screen reader setup.

speaker: ALEX
text: Put Step 2 - Accept the GitHub Classroom Assignment into plain language. At the start of Day 1, the facilitator gives you a GitHub Classroom assignment link. The useful version is: It usually starts with https://classroom.github.com/a/. The interface gets easier when it becomes a set of named places instead of a wall of controls.

speaker: ALEX
text: Open the assignment link in the browser where you are signed in to GitHub; If GitHub asks you to authorize GitHub Classroom, activate Authorize GitHub Classroom; If you are asked to choose your name from a roster, find your name and select it. If your name is missing, use the skip option and tell the facilitator; and Activate Accept this assignment.

speaker: ALEX
text: Think of this as 3 checks: Wait while GitHub Classroom creates your private repository; Refresh the page until the repository link appears; and Open the repository link and bookmark it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the learner is not behind if they stop there and check the page.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Pausing to verify is not a detour; it is how you keep control of the workflow.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Okay, set the room for us. What are we walking into?

speaker: ALEX
text: The Learning Room is a private repository created from a template. Everyone starts from the same materials, but your work belongs to you.

speaker: ALEX
text: For a learner, the useful signals are concrete. You have your own issues, branches, commits, and pull requests. Other students do not see your work unless the facilitator intentionally pairs you. Mistakes are expected and recoverable. Bot feedback is educational, not punitive.

speaker: ALEX
text: After your Learning Room repository is created, the Student Progression Bot creates your first challenge issue. When you close a challenge issue, the next challenge opens.

speaker: ALEX
text: Step one is open your Learning Room repository. Step two is navigate to the Issues tab. On GitHub, the keyboard shortcut is G then I. Step three is find an issue titled Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around. Step four is open the issue and read the body from top to bottom.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on Step 4 - Find Challenge 1. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: First, follow the checklist in the issue. Then, post your evidence in the evidence field or as the requested comment. After that, close the challenge issue when the instructions tell you to close it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What stays the same when the tool changes?

speaker: ALEX
text: Step 5 - Choose the Tool That Fits the Moment: There is no single correct way to use GitHub. The workshop teaches the workflow first, then offers tool paths.

speaker: ALEX
text: GitHub.com in the browser: Best for Day 1, issues, pull requests, repository navigation, and reviews. github.dev: Best when you want a VS Code-style editor in the browser without installing anything. Press the period key from many repository pages to open it. VS Code desktop: Best for Day 2, local Git, Copilot, extensions, and deeper editing work. GitHub Desktop: Best if you want a desktop Git workflow without typing Git commands.

speaker: ALEX
text: Here is the practical turn. When you feel lost, listen for structure before you take action. If you are not sure where you are, pause and navigate by headings or landmarks.

speaker: ALEX
text: On the ground, that means a few things. Page title. Repository name heading. Landmark names such as main content or repository navigation. Tab names such as Code, Issues, and Pull requests.

speaker: ALEX
text: A solid navigation habit is to prove where you are before activating controls. Headings, landmarks, and the address bar are not trivia; they are your map.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do the two days connect instead of feeling like separate courses?

speaker: ALEX
text: if something does not work, do not start over silently. Read the latest bot message, check the challenge issue, and ask for help with the link to the page where you are stuck.

speaker: ALEX
text: These are the details that keep the idea from floating away. Every challenge issue includes instructions and evidence prompts. Every chapter has an If You Get Stuck section. Every challenge has a reference solution in the solutions folder. Gandalf posts feedback on pull requests.

text: That is a useful checkpoint before anyone starts pressing keys.

speaker: ALEX
text: You are ready to continue when you can say these four things. This is the part to say slowly: You do not need to understand every GitHub feature before you begin.

speaker: ALEX
text: Think of this as 4 checks: I can open my Learning Room repository; I can find the Issues tab; I can open Challenge 1; and I know where to post my evidence and how to ask for help. Keep it that plain: know where you are, make the move, check the result.

speaker: ALEX
text: Carry the map. Know what page or tool you are in, know which action you are taking, and know what confirmation should follow. If the confirmation is missing, pause. That pause is not wasted time; it is professional judgment.
